title: Three Measures
context: Grade 5, the closing pages. An adult sees a checklist, a vocabulary list, an open investigation and a water activity. What the pages are doing is bringing the three measures together: a length, a surface and a space, each in its own unit; every cuboid of a set of cubes found once; and a volume shown by the water a solid pushes aside when it is fully under.

writeup.why: Tell perimeter, area and volume apart by what they measure and by their units, find every cuboid of a set of cubes once, and compare volumes by rising water with every object fully under.
writeup.look: Three measure bins with their units on the first phase, a cube tray and a cuboid shelf on the second, and equal jars of water with the Push stick on the last two.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Three Measures' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of cards sorted, cuboids shelved or levels marked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. On the first phase the three bins stand along y 480 at x 120, x 440 and x 760, each 280 by 200, labelled Length, Surface and Space in ink with their units under them; the cards wait in a row along y 230, and the unit tiles in a tray along y 700. On the second phase the heap of violet unit cubes, labelled Unit cube, lies at x 120, y 560, the tray for building at x 120, y 260, the Turn button at x 540, y 260, and the shelf runs along y 400 from x 600, 480 long; a turned copy set on the shelf slides onto its twin and the two are labelled Same cuboid. On the last two phases the equal clear jars stand at x 200 and x 560, each 220 by 380, with a near-black line at the starting level; Mark level draws the new line and the rise between the two is lit green. The Push stick is a thin rod at x 900, y 260 that the child drags onto a floating object to hold it fully under. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with unit keys for cm, sq. cm and cu. cm. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The bins stay filled with their cards and units, the shelf with its cuboids, and the jars with their marked levels.

writeup.delight: On the second phase, when a turned copy slides onto its twin on the shelf, the two give a little bump together like old friends meeting.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet moved. On the first phase the three bins stand across the working area with the cards in a row above them. On the second a heap of unit cubes waits beside the tray and an empty shelf. On the third two equal jars stand filled to one line with two objects beside them. On the fourth a jar stands filled to its line with a cork bobbing at the top and the Push stick beside it. One thing moves, once: the first card, the heap of cubes or the water in the jars gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any card sorted, any cuboid built and turned, and any object lowered or pushed under. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on which measure and unit, cuboids of a set of cubes, rising water and floaters.

observations.why: a length, a surface and a space are three different measures.
observations.soWhat: name what is measured first, then pick its unit.
observations.observe: Every card went into exactly one bin, and each bin had its own kind of unit.

observations.why: turning a cuboid onto another face does not change its length, breadth or height, only which way it stands.
observations.soWhat: each cuboid is counted once, and a turned cuboid is the same cuboid.
observations.observe: A turned cuboid set on the shelf slid onto a cuboid already there.

observations.why: an object fully under pushes aside as much water as the space it takes up.
observations.soWhat: in equal jars with equal water, the greater rise shows the greater volume.
observations.observe: The water rose more for the bigger object.

observations.why: a floating cork is only partly under the water, so it pushes aside less.
observations.soWhat: push a floating object fully under before reading the rise.
observations.observe: The cork's rise grew when it was pushed fully under.

serves.exercise: ticking the self-assessment list of can-dos
making flashcards for eight vocabulary words
building every cuboid that twelve unit cubes can make and recording its measurements
comparing the volumes of four objects by how far the water rises

source_tool.description: On the first phase three bins stand across the working area, labelled Length, Surface and Space, with the units cm and m, sq. cm and sq. m, and cu. cm and cu. m written under them. Cards showing things to be measured, a fence, a lawn, a tank, a ribbon, and the chapter's word cards are dragged into a bin, and a unit is dragged onto each. On the second phase a heap of violet unit cubes, each labelled Unit cube, is built into cuboids on a tray; a Turn button stands the cuboid on another face, and a shelf keeps each cuboid the child sets on it. A turned copy set on the shelf slides onto its twin and the two are labelled Same cuboid. On the last two phases equal clear jars hold water to one marked line; the child lowers an object into a jar and taps Mark level to draw the new line, with the rise lit green. A floating object bobs at the top until the Push stick holds it fully under. A number pad types a count or a unit. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of cards sorted, cuboids shelved or levels marked.
source_tool.art_direction: Jars of water on a windowsill / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line

zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look again. Is it a length, a surface or a space?
voice.onNext: Something new to sort, build or lower in.
voice.opening: Three bins, some cubes and some jars of water.
voice.onFinish: You told the three measures apart and read the water.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Sort, build and lower anything you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has built cuboids from real cubes and lowered a stone into a jar of water. The tool is what keeps each cuboid once on a shelf and pushes a floater fully under, so the two slips the closing pages invite are seen and fixed.

answer_key.rule: A perimeter is a length, in cm or m. An area is a surface, in square units such as sq. cm or sq. m. A volume is a space, in cubic units such as cu. cm or cu. m. Every cuboid of a set of cubes is found by looking for three whole numbers that multiply to the count, and each is counted once: standing a cuboid on another face does not make a new cuboid, it is the same cuboid, turned. A solid lowered fully under water raises the water by as much space as it takes up. A floating object is only partly under, so push it fully under with a thin stick before reading the rise, and use equal jars holding equal water.
answer_key.wrong: The child's card, cuboid or level mark stays where it was put, and the stage sets the right bin, the twin on the shelf or the fully-under level beside it, lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The fence runs along the boundary, so it is a length, in m.
The grass covers a surface, so it is an area, in sq. m.
The water fills a space, so it is a volume, in cu. m.
items.answer: The fence in m, the grass in sq. m, and the water in cu. m
items.question: Which unit fits each: the fence round a field, the grass inside it, and the water in a tank?
items.checkpoint: Name what is measured first: a length, a surface or a space.
items.misconception: Giving the grass in m, a unit of length, though grass covers a surface.

steps: Look for three whole numbers that multiply to 18.
One is 18 long, 1 wide and 1 high.
One is 9 long, 2 wide and 1 high.
One is 6 long, 3 wide and 1 high.
One is 3 long, 3 wide and 2 high.
Standing any of them on another face gives the same cuboid, turned, so there are 4 different cuboids.
items.question: How many different cuboids can 18 unit cubes make?
items.checkpoint: A cuboid turned onto another face is the same cuboid.
items.misconception: Counting a cuboid again after standing it on another face, though a turned cuboid is the same cuboid.

steps: Each object pushes water out of its way, so the water rises by as much space as the object takes up.
The jars are equal and hold equal water, so the rises can be compared.
The stone's water rose more, so the stone has the greater volume.
items.question: Two equal jars hold equal water. A key goes into one and a stone into the other, both fully under. The stone's jar rises more. Which has the greater volume?
items.checkpoint: The rise shows the space an object takes up.
items.misconception: Choosing the key because it is longer, though the rise shows the space an object takes up, not its length.

steps: A floating cork is only partly under the water.
Push it fully under with a thin stick.
Then read how far the water has risen, which now shows all the space the cork takes up.
Use equal jars holding equal water, so rises can be compared.
items.answer: Push it fully under with a thin stick, then read the rise
items.question: A cork floats in a jar of water. How can the rise show its volume?
items.checkpoint: Push it fully under before reading the rise.
items.misconception: Reading the rise while the cork floats, which shows only the part under the water.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Is the space inside a box measured in cm, sq. cm or cu. cm?
items.final_answer: cu. cm, because a volume is a space

items.question: A cuboid 5 long, 2 wide and 1 high is stood on its end. Is it a new cuboid?
items.final_answer: No. It is the same cuboid, turned

items.question: Two equal jars hold equal water. A marble goes into one, and a lemon, pushed fully under, into the other. The lemon's jar rises more. Which has the greater volume?
Is the grass inside a fence a perimeter, an area or a volume?
items.final_answer: An area, measured in square units such as sq. m

items.question: How many different cuboids can 7 unit cubes make?
items.final_answer: Only one: a row 7 long, 1 wide and 1 high. Turning it does not make a new cuboid

items.question: Why is a floating ball pushed fully under before the rise is read?
items.final_answer: A floating ball is only partly under the water. Only when it is fully under does the rise show all the space it takes up

items.question: How many different cuboids can 8 unit cubes make?
items.final_answer: 3. One is 8 long, 1 wide and 1 high. One is 4 long, 2 wide and 1 high. One is 2 long, 2 wide and 2 high, which is a cube

items.question: Two equal jars hold equal water. A plastic ball floats in one, not held under, and the water rises only a little. Does that small rise show the ball's volume?
items.final_answer: No. The ball is only partly under the water. Push it fully under, then read the rise

teaching_notes: Sort measures by what they measure, a length, a surface or a space, before naming any unit. Build cuboids with real cubes and turn each one to see that it stays the same cuboid; count each shape once. Lower a stone into a jar of water before the tool opens. Push every object fully under the water before reading the rise; a floating object shows its volume only when it is held fully under. The self-assessment is the child's own, so let each can-do be ticked honestly. The printed set of cubes and the printed objects are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build a three measures tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Three bins, labelled Length, Surface and Space with their units, take cards of things to be measured and the chapter's word cards, and unit tiles are dragged onto the cards. A heap of violet unit cubes, labelled Unit cube, is built into cuboids on a tray; a Turn button stands a cuboid on another face, and a shelf keeps each cuboid once, a turned copy sliding onto its twin labelled Same cuboid. Equal clear jars hold water to one marked line; an object lowered in raises the water, and a Mark level button draws the new line with the rise lit green. A floating object bobs at the top until a Push stick holds it fully under. A number pad types counts. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the cards sorted, cuboids shelved or levels marked. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
